Title: 12 Questions to Ask Your Prospective Monitoring & Enforcement Vendor | Friend MTS
Does your vendor have a monitoring solution proven to disrupt revenue-damaging content fraud? To protect your revenue effectively, content monitoring and enforcement must deliver both comprehensive detection and meaningful disruption of piracy. A qualified content protection vendor should be able to conduct a comprehensive audit to assess the scale and nature of your piracy exposure. By using specialised technologies and curated intelligence and insights gathered from years of experience protecting high-value live and on-demand content, an expert provider should be able to detect piracy across a wide range of sources and clearly outline the scope of the threat to your business. Once you have ensured that your vendor is an established content protection expert and a trusted member of a wide network of organisations in the content security ecosystem, it’s time to ask the ‘deeper dive’ questions that will help you understand whether this vendor’s solutions suit your revenue protection needs. As a result, legitimate service providers need to ensure that their content protection and anti-piracy solutions are robust against vulnerabilities. Make sure that your vendor has the depth of expertise and technology required to accurately discover, capture, map and analyse the constantly evolving tactics employed by pirates, not only to steal content, but also to circumvent the technology designed to protect it. While it’s important to make sure valuable content is protected from fraud and illegal redistribution, legitimate content owners and service providers partnering with an anti-piracy company must make sure that takedowns are accurate, especially when large volumes of content are involved. Does your vendor address all major sources of content fraud or just open web? If your content is being redistributed illegally across multiple channels, ensure your vendor has a proven track record of detecting and disrupting piracy across all of them – not just the most visible ones. Many of these platforms have built-in rights management solutions (e.g. Facebook’s Right Manager, YouTube’s Content ID, etc.), so it’s crucial your vendor operates a compliance programme with these to ensure that takedowns are swift. It’s also worth checking if your vendor has proven relationships and enforcement processes for effective takedowns with regional social media platforms, ensuring faster removal of infringing content across all markets.

results.title: How Often Should Fraud Detection Rules be Reviewed to Maintain Accuracy?
results.content: Fraud detection rules refer to a set of predefined criteria – based on behavioral analytics, patterns, or risk thresholds – that flag suspicious activities and enable businesses to take swift action to prevent fraud. Optimizing detection rules is a critical, ongoing process that uses the latest digital technologies for real-time data integration, customer profiling, and continuous learning. The other techniques that help refine fraud detection rules include machine learning and data analytics to dynamically identify nuanced patterns, behavioral analytics for real-time risk scoring of every user, feedback loops to ensure detection criteria evolve based on new fraud trends, and contextual decision-making to minimize false positives without compromising accuracy. It provides businesses with real-time insights into emerging fraud tactics, enabling them to proactively update fraud detection rules and refine risk thresholds to reduce false positives and adapt to evolving fraud tactics.

results.title: Internal Audit Points to Fraud in D.C. Housing Authority Voucher Program - Internal Audit 360
results.content: # Internal Audit Points to Fraud in D.C. Housing Authority Voucher Program. Reports of mismanagement and voucher fraud at the D.C. Housing Authority (DCHA) continue to pile up, At-large Councilmember Robert White insisted at a press conference on March 30. White, who has chaired the council’s Housing Committee since January, highlighted four instances of alleged wrongdoing within DCHA — three of which were already investigated by DCHA and have been the subject of news coverage — to point to systemic issues at the agency, which oversees D.C.’s public housing and voucher programs. Speaking to reporters after White’s press conference, DCHA Director Brenda Donald acknowledged the findings but said there was no indication of pervasive fraud in the agency. Audit reports for two of the allegations found that a lack of checks and balances — as well as poor supervision of new employees, management failures and an inadequate understanding of program rules — could have contributed to the issues. # Article Categories.
